1299-the-heritage-of-the-sioux:
B. M. Bower sets this western among the Sioux country, where a young cowboy inherits a ranch and a feud, and must win the trust of his neighbors, white and Indian alike. The tale moves through roundups, rustlers, and a love that crosses the old lines of the range.

Bower writes cowboy life with humor and a woman's eye for character, and her Sioux country is drawn with respect rare for its day. The novel is brisk and warm. It suits readers who like westerns with strong people and a real sense of place.
1305-the-ball-at-sceaux:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Emilie de Fontaine, a proud young beauty who scorns every suitor at the ball at Sceaux. She holds out for a peer of France, and she falls for a mysterious stranger whose true rank hides a surprise. The tale follows her pride to its comic fall.

Balzac writes Parisian society with wit and a sharp eye for snobbery, and the story turns on a single, well-placed irony. The tale is short and sparkling. It suits readers who like Balzac's comedies of vanity and love.
20863-major-vigoureux:
Sergeant Archelaus digs in a neglected garden as Major Vigoureux opens in talk of trousers. The Commandant's sharp query halts the long man mid-spade. He grounds his spade like a musket and stands to face the charge.

Arthur Quiller-Couch sets this tale of 1907 among the Scilly Isles' small garrison. An ageing major, a dull post, and a sudden call to act drive the plot. Q, as readers called him, blends humour with a seaman's love of Cornwall's coasts. The book charms with its gentle pace before duty turns the quiet post upside down.
341-myths-and-legends-of-the-sioux:
Marie McLaughlin, who states she is of one-fourth Sioux blood, retells stories she heard from her mother in this short book. The tales come from Sioux home life and camp lore, and many turn on animals, tricksters, and brave deeds. Unktomi the spider, the rabbit, the bear, and the crow recur through the set.

Stories tell how the rabbit lost his tail, how corn came as a gift, and how the peace pipe took its place in Sioux custom. Others praise faithful lovers, lone warriors, and wise fools. Told in plain, brief prose, the book keeps old tales in a form a child or a new reader can follow with ease.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-cite:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Cîteaux describes the mother house of the Cistercian Order. St. Robert, Abbot of Molesme, founded it in 1098. Robert and twenty companions settled a deserted, marshy place in the diocese of Châlons, where rushes called cistels gave the site its name.

There they began the literal observance of St. Benedict's Rule, in a new monastery distinguished from Molesme, on land given by Raynald, Viscount of Beaune, and his wife Hodierna. The name Cîteaux soon replaced Novum Monasterium, and the order that grew from this marshy valley spread across Europe. The entry traces the foundation, its patrons and the beginnings of Cistercian life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-clai:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clairvaux describes the third daughter of Cîteaux. St. Bernard founded it in 1115 in a deep Aube valley, then called the Valley of Wormwood. Hughes the First, Count of Troyes, gave the valley to the Cistercian colony. By a charter of 1116 the house is already called Clara Vallis, or Clairvaux.

After a trying beginning, Clairvaux grew rapidly under Bernard, whose renown drew so many postulants that in his lifetime it planted sixty-eight daughter houses. Those houses stood across France, Italy, Germany, England, Spain and Portugal. Colonies went to Trois-Fontaines in 1116 and to Fontenay in 1119. The entry follows Clairvaux's astonishing expansion under its great abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnulf-of-lis:
Arnulf of Lisieux, called Lexoviensis or Luxoviensis, died on 31 August 1184 after a career in law, crusade, and church politics. Educated by his brother, bishop of Séez, he studied canon law at Rome and wrote a letter for Pope Innocent II against Gerard of Angoulême, partisan of Antipope Anacletus II. Raised to Lisieux in 1141, he joined Louis VII's crusade in 1147 and stayed faithful to Alexander III during schism. He urged fellow bishops to defend church liberty against Henry II of England.

He backed the king, however, in the quarrel between Henry and Thomas Becket, and after Becket's murder undertook the king's defence before the pope. In 1181 or a little earlier he lost favour with king and, for a time, with Pope Lucius, then resigned his see for age and feebleness and retired to St. Victor's Abbey at Paris, where he died. His letters, collected by himself, survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bayeux:
Bayeux is a diocese coextensive with Calvados, suffragan to Rouen, joined to ancient Lisieux at the Concordat of 1862. An 1854 brief lets its bishop style himself Bishop of Bayeux and Lisieux. Legend makes St Exuperius, a disciple of Clement, its first-century founder, but Bollandists and Jules Lair show he founded the see only in the mid-fourth century. Saintly successors include Lupus about 465, Vigor, who destroyed a still-frequented pagan temple, and Regnobertus about 629.

Hugues, who died in 730, held Paris and Rouen besides Bayeux. Odon of Conteville (1050-97), William the Conqueror's brother, built the cathedral, attended Hastings, and died a crusader in Sicily. In 1641 Jean Eudes founded Caen's Our Lady of Charity and Refuge for young girls, now holding thirty-three monasteries. Diocesan missionaries at Notre Dame de la Déliverande direct educational institutions across the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benoit-marie-:
Benoît-Marie Langénieux, cardinal and Archbishop of Reims, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Villefranche-sur-Saône in 1824, he died at Reims in 1905 after a steady climb through Paris parishes. Ordained in 1850, he served as curate, diocesan promoter, parish priest, and vicar-general of Paris before becoming Bishop of Tarbes in 1873.

Translated to Reims the next year, he held the see for thirty-one fruitful years. He won state funds for restoring the cathedral, fostered pilgrimages and Catholic schools, and was named cardinal. The entry presents a builder-archbishop who restored the prestige of the coronation city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bordeaux:
Bordeaux, archdiocese of the whole Gironde department, was rebuilt by the Concordat of 1802 from the old Bordeaux diocese and most of suppressed Bazas. It became metropolitan over Angouleme, Poitiers, and La Rochelle, gaining Agen, Perigueux, and Lucon in 1822 and three colonial sees, Martinique, Guadeloupe, and Reunion, in 1850.

Limousin legend credits Saint Martial with evangelizing Bordeaux in the first century, but the first bishop known to history is Orientalis, named at Arles in 314. By the late fourth century the faith had grown enough for a synod against the Priscillianists in 385. Delphinus, bishop from 380 to 404, wrote to Ambrose and Paulinus of Nola. Seurin held the see from 410 to 420 after Amand abdicated for him, and Leontius II, bishop from 542 to 564, spent his wealth on churches and land clearance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-batte:
Charles Batteux was an abbé and writer on philosophy and aesthetics, born near Vouziers in 1713 and dead at Paris in 1780. He taught humanities and rhetoric at Paris, then Greek and Roman philosophy. He joined both the Academy of Inscriptions and the Académie Française. His writings on Epicurus and other Greek philosophers drew wide attention. At his death he was publishing memoirs on China, later continued by Bréquigny and de Guignes.

Three works won him equal praise and blame: his reduction of the fine arts to one principle, his course of polite letters, and his treatise on oratory. They were later gathered into five volumes, then reissued in six in 1824. Following Aristotle, though one-sidedly, he derived art from the free imitation of nature in its beautiful forms. Utility marks the mechanical arts and beauty the fine arts. The beautifying arts, including architecture and oratory, aim at both.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crusade-of-th:
This historical entry recounts the Crusade of the Pastoureaux, or Shepherds, one of the strangest popular movements to free the Holy Land. When St. Louis of France was captured in Egypt in 1250, his mother Blanche of Castile could win no reinforcements from nobles or clergy. Shepherds and labourers then rose, vowing to rescue their king.

About Easter 1251 a mysterious preacher called the Master of Hungary began preaching the Crusade in northern France. With long beard, thin face, and a hand said to hold a map from the Virgin, he drew crowds and handed out crosses without Church licence. An army of 30,000 formed and marched, but soon turned hostile to clergy, above all the Dominicans. The movement collapsed into violence, and a second rising in 1320 is also covered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evreux:
Evreux is a diocese in the Department of Eure in France, suffragan to the Archbishopric of Rouen. Legend makes Saint Taurinus its first bishop. He was baptized at Rome by Saint Clement and sent into Gaul with Saint Denis. But Duchesne traces the tale to the ninth century, when Abbot Hilduin sought to identify Dionysius the Areopagite with Denis of Paris. The first bishop known to history is Maurusio, present at Orléans's council in 511. Later bishops include Gilbert, who preached the funeral oration over William the Conqueror, and Du Perron, a chief agent in the abjuration of Henry IV.

In 1905 the diocese counted 334,781 souls, 37 parishes, 545 mission churches, and 25 vicariates on state pay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-c:
Geoffrey of Clairvaux, disciple and secretary of Saint Bernard, was born at Auxerre between 1115 and 1120. He first heard Abelard's lectures at Paris, then heard Bernard preach conversion to the clergy in 1140 and followed him to Clairvaux with several fellow scholars. Soon he won the abbot's trust as his notary and constant companion.

Geoffrey traveled with Bernard to Toulouse against heresy in 1145 and through France and Germany preaching crusade in 1146 and 1147. He became abbot of Igny in 1159 and fourth abbot of Clairvaux in 1162, resigning in 1165, then ruled Fossa Nuova from 1170 and Haute Combe from 1176. His chief work remains Bernard's five-book life, built from his own notes and revisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-buteu:
French missionary Jacques Buteux was born at Abbeville, Picardy, on 11 April 1600. He was killed by Iroquois on 10 May 1652. He entered the Society of Jesus in October 1620. He studied at La Flèche from 1622 to 1625. He taught at Caen from 1625 to 1629. After theology at La Flèche, he became prefect at Clermont college. In 1634 he sailed to Canada.

He was sent to the new settlement of Three Rivers. There he stayed eighteen years, serving Montagnais and Algonquin peoples with extraordinary zeal. Though frail in body, he burned with desire for suffering. No peril, however great, ever paled his cheek or stayed his hand in serving God or saving souls. The entry presents a delicate man whose courage marked him among heroic missioners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-devereux:
John Devereux was a pioneer merchant of Utica, New York, remembered as a prince among his fellows for charity and public spirit. Born at The Leap near Enniscorthy in Ireland in 1774, he came of a patriotic and pious family. A brother fought in the Rebellion of 1798 with a price on his head, another died at Vinegar Hill, and a sister became superioress of the Presentation Convent at Enniscorthy.

Landing at New York about 1797, Devereux taught dancing in Connecticut. He opened a store at Utica in 1802, grew wealthy, and was elected the city's first mayor in 1840. With his brother Nicholas he founded the Utica Savings Bank and brought the Sisters of Charity to open an orphanage, each brother giving five thousand dollars. Missionary priests always stayed at his house, where local Catholics heard Sunday Mass, and he died at Utica in 1848.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-marcou:
Joseph Marcoux was a Canadian missionary who spent forty-two years among the Iroquois. Born in Canada in 1791 and ordained in 1813, he worked at St. Regis, then at Caughnawaga (Sault-St-Louis), until his death from typhoid fever in 1855. He gave his flock a church and schools in 1845.

Marcoux mastered the Iroquois tongue so well that his grammar and French-Iroquois dictionary won him rank among philologists. For his people he translated a Life of Christ and published prayers, hymns, a catechism, a ritual calendar, and sermons in their own language. The entry honors a pastor who served one people for a lifetime.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurence-vaux:
Laurence Vaux (1519-1585) was a canon regular, catechism author, and martyr in prison, born at Blackrod, Lancashire. Schooled at Manchester and Oxford, ordained in 1542, he became fellow and then warden of Manchester College in 1558.

When Elizabeth's commissioners visited in 1559, Vaux hid himself with the college deeds and plate. He then fled to Louvain in 1561, keeping a school for English exiles' children and writing his catechism for them. Pius V's ruling that attending Established services was mortal sin reached England largely through Vaux. He campaigned against conforming practice in Lancashire until a 1568 writ forced him back to Louvain. At fifty-four he joined the canons regular of St. Martin's, guarding the college deeds for a restored Catholic college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loucheux:
The Loucheux, who call themselves Dindjye, or men, are a confederation of closely kin tribes, the most north-western branch of the Dene peoples. Their land runs from the Anderson River eastward to the far west of Alaska, covering nearly all the Alaskan interior.

Fourteen tribes make up the group, from the Willow River people and the Coyukons on the Yukon to the Crow People, the River People, and the Mackenzie people on the Arctic fringe. The name Loucheux, French for cross-eyed, came from one tribe between the Porcupine headwaters and Fort McPherson, then spread to all. Mission work, trade, and Eskimo neighbours shape the later pages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meaux:
Meaux, a French diocese covering the whole department of Seine-et-Marne, was suffragan of Sens until 1622 and then of Paris. The Concordat of 1801 first gave it the Marne department, later split off to Reims and Chalons in 1821 and 1822. Today's diocese joins most of old Meaux with large parts of old Sens, parts of Paris, and parishes from Troyes, Soissons, and Senlis.

Hildegaire, writing in the ninth century, calls St. Faro the twentieth bishop since St. Denis, whom tradition names first bishop, followed by St. Saintin and St. Antoninus. A document shown to Charles the Bald in 876 or 877 tells how Antoninus and Saintin carried news of Denis's martyrdom to Pope Anacletus. Duchesne, however, names Medovechus, present at two councils, as the first historically certain bishop. The entry weighs tradition against record across the see's long line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-levad:
Michael Levadoux was among the first Sulpicians who, when religion lay distressed in France, crossed to the United States and founded St. Mary's Seminary in Baltimore. He was born at Clermont-Ferrand in Auvergne on 1 April 1746 and died at Le-Puy-en-Velay on 13 January 1815. He entered the Sulpician seminary at Clermont in 1769, studied theology, and spent a year in the Solitude novitiate.

In 1774 he became director of the Limoges seminary, staying until 1791. As affairs darkened in France, Superior-General Emery resolved to plant a Sulpician house abroad, and at Nuncio Dugnani's suggestion chose the United States. After talks with Bishop Carroll, Francis Nagot was named first director of the planned Baltimore seminary. Levadoux sailed with Nagot's party from St. Malo on 8 April 1791 and reached Baltimore on 10 July, after a stormy, roundabout voyage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-deve:
Nicholas Devereux, born near Enniscorthy, Ireland, on 7 June 1791 and dead at Utica, New York, on 29 December 1855, was the youngest brother of John C. Devereux. Reaching New York in 1806, he attended Mass at Saint Peter's, Barclay Street, on his first Sunday, putting one of his last three gold coins on the plate. God blessed his generosity, and fifty years later he had amassed half a million dollars as a merchant.

He bought 400,000 acres from the Holland Land Company in Allegheny and Cattaraugus counties, New York, and founded an Irish settlement there. He gave largely to churches, colleges and charitable institutions. Visiting Rome in 1854 with his wife, daughter Mary and Reverend Michael Clarke, he brought six Franciscan Fathers to America. He gave $10,000 toward their Allegheny monastery, now Saint Bonaventure college and seminary. His widow later fulfilled his wish for an American seminary at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-boile:
Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux, the French poet and critic born at Paris in 1636, gave French verse its rules and French letters its first steady criticism. Trained for the church, then for the law, he lived on a family inheritance and gave himself wholly to poetry from the age of twenty-one.

His early satires mocked weak writers and, in imitation of Horace and Juvenal, set out how French lines should scan and how poems should be judged. Later works, with a treatise on the art of poetry, made him the age's arbiter of taste until his death in 1711.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-letou:
French preacher Nicolas Letourneux, born at Rouen in 1640, moved from Jansenist rigor to a steadier pastoral path. Poor parents and rich patrons carried him through Jesuit schooling in Paris, and he was ordained at Rouen in 1662 before joining the Port-Royal circle.

For a time he wore a coarse grey robe and stopped saying Mass to atone for early ordination. Friends drew him back to parish work, his sermons placed him among Paris's finest preachers, and a 1675 sermon on Martha won the French Academy's Balzac prize for eloquence. Wealthy benefactors paid for his schooling after his poor parents could not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perigueux:
Périgueux was a French diocese covering the Dordogne, suffragan to Bordeaux. Joined to Angoulême by the Concordat of 1801, it regained its own bishop in 1821. The restored see reunited old Périgueux and Sarlat, minus parishes given to Agen, Angoulême, Limoges, Cahors, and Tulle. Tradition names St. Front its first bishop, sent by St. Peter, though later lives blend him with an Egyptian Fronto.

Recorded history begins with Bishop Paternus, deposed for heresy about 361. Later bishops include the cardinals of Pons and Givry, Blessed Elie de Bourdeilles, and the future Cardinal Gousset. The entry also covers Sarlat's abbey of Saint-Sauveur, reformed by St. Odo of Cluny about 936 and raised to a bishopric by John XXII in 1318.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-therese:
Therese of Lisieux, the Little Flower, was born at Alençon on 2 January 1873 and died at Lisieux on 30 September 1897, aged only twenty-four. Ninth child of Louis and Zélie Martin, who had themselves longed for the cloister, she grew up in a household where faith shaped every day. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, written soon after her death, captures a fame already spreading fast.

At fifteen she sought the Carmelite convent and, refused by the superior, travelled to Rome with her father to plead with Leo XIII during his jubilee. The pope left the choice to the superior, who at last consented, and Therese entered on 9 April 1888. The entry traces her short convent life of hidden prayer, and explains why readers far beyond Normandy were already turning to her story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigebert-of-g:
Sigebert of Gembloux, a Benedictine historian born near Gembloux, now in Namur province, about 1035, died there on 5 November 1112. He seems to have been of Latin descent rather than German. He was schooled at Gembloux abbey, became a monk there young, and taught for a long time at Saint Vincent's abbey at Metz. About 1070 he returned to Gembloux, where he was admired and venerated and ran the abbey school until his death.

At Metz he wrote lives of Bishop Theodoric I and King Sigebert III. Back at Gembloux he wrote on the Theban Legion, a life of the founder Wicbert, and a history of the abbots. Later he turned imperial partisan in the empire-papacy struggle. His great chronicle and his list of church writers crown the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-caryll-mo:
Caryll Molyneux, Baronet of Sefton and third Viscount Molyneux of Maryborough in Ireland, was born in 1624 and died in 1699. He joined the Royalist army at the civil war's outbreak and served with his brother in the mostly Catholic Lancashire Regiment from Manchester in 1642 to Worcester in 1651. After succeeding to the title, he suffered harsh treatment from the victors as a known Catholic cavalier.

Fortunes improved only under James II, when he became Lord Lieutenant of Lancashire and seized and held Chester for James against the Prince of Orange. Years later he was arrested on a trumped-up treason charge, jailed in the Tower, and acquitted at trial in 1694.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bernard-of:
St. Bernard of Clairvaux was born in 1090 at Fontaines near Dijon in France. He died at Clairvaux on 21 August 1153. This entry follows a boy whose parents, Tescelin, lord of Fontaines, and Aleth of Montbard, both belonged to the highest nobility of Burgundy. Bernard, third of seven children, received an education of particular care: while yet unborn, a devout man had foretold his great destiny.

At nine, Bernard went to a much renowned school at Chatillon-sur-Seine, run by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles. He loved literature and devoted himself for some time to poetry. His success in study won his masters' admiration, and his virtue grew no less. Bernard most desired to excel in literature, so that he could take up Sacred Scripture, which later became, as it were, his own tongue. Piety was his all, says Bossuet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
During the English domination of Aquitaine, Bordeaux gained its university in 1441 under King Henry VI. A bull of Pope Eugenius IV founded it at the request of the archbishop's officials and the Aquitanian councillors, with Pierre Berland then archbishop. The king himself did not officially recognize it until the reign of Louis XI. Under its bull it was organized on the model of Toulouse, with the Archbishop of Bordeaux as chancellor for life.

It held all the faculties: theology, canon law, civil law, arts, and more. Yet constant lack of endowment kept it from any remarkable standing from its founding to the French Revolution. After the Revolution the universities were reorganized, and Bordeaux shared the new pattern. The entry gives a compact history of a provincial university that survived more by endurance than by fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-alexan:
Victor Alexandre Puiseux was a French mathematician and astronomer who lived from 1820 to 1883. Schooled at Pont-à-Mousson, then in Paris, he won lycée prizes in mathematics and physics, entered the École Normale in 1837, took his doctorate in mathematical sciences in 1841. Taught at Rennes, Besançon, and the École Normale, substituting at the Sorbonne and Collège de France for Sturm, Le Verrier, and Binet.

From 1855 to 1859 he served as assistant astronomer at the Paris Observatory, heading its bureau of calculation under Le Verrier. From 1857 until six months before his death he held Cauchy's chair of celestial mechanics at the Sorbonne, keeping the title after resigning. He also belonged to the Bureau des Longitudes from 1868 to 1872, and his work in celestial mechanics and analysis made him a central figure of French mathematical astronomy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ch:
William of Champeaux was a twelfth-century Paris teacher and bishop famed for his doctrine of universals. Born at Champeaux near Melun about 1070, he died at Châlons-sur-Marne in 1121. Pupil of Anselm of Laon, he began teaching at the Paris cathedral school in 1103. Abelard's attacks on his strong realist view, that shared natures are real, drove him in 1108 to Saint Victor's Abbey, feeding the Victorine mystic school. He became Bishop of Châlons in 1114.

On universals William shifted ground, yet always toward exaggerated realism, against Roscelin's nominalism, that names are mere words, and Abelard's softened version. Surviving pieces include parts of De Origine Animae, a book of sentences, and a Christian-Jewish dialogue. In the soul treatise he rejects traducianism, the passing of souls from parents, holding instead that God creates each soul directly. Peers prized him as the ablest champion of orthodoxy.
myths-and-legends-of-the-sioux:
Marie L. McLaughlin dedicates these Sioux tales to her mother's memory. Most stories here were told to her at her mother's knee. The contents open with the Forgotten Ear of Corn. The Little Mice and the Pet Rabbit follow.

Rabbit tales run through the book, meeting elk, bears, and grouse girls. The Legend of Standing Rock and the Peace Pipe story anchor the set. Unktomi the trickster loses his tail in one tale. Faithful lovers, lost wives, and a lone warrior fill out the list. McLaughlin, of Sioux heritage herself, saved oral tales in print for new generations.
phineas-redux: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Phineas Redux, an editorial note and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The note records that Anthony Trollope's novel ran in the Graphic from July 1873 to January 1874. It appeared in book form from Chapman and Hall in 1874, with illustrations by Frank Holl. The contents open with Temptation, Harrington Hall, and Phineas among his old friends, returning the Irish member to Parliament.
the-ball-at-sceaux:
Honore de Balzac's tale, translated by Clara Bell, centres on the Comte de Fontaine, head of an old Poitou family. Fontaine served the Bourbon cause in the Vendee war and was left for dead at Les Quatre Chemins. Ruined by confiscation, he refused posts offered by Napoleon.

Faithful to his class, he married a penniless woman from an old Breton family rather than a rich upstart's kin. In Paris with a large family, he receives rank and crosses he did not seek. Those favours shake his plan to return home and draw him toward a private audience with the king.
the-heritage-of-the-sioux:
B. M. Bower wrote The Heritage of the Sioux. The contents list twenty-one chapters, among them When Green Grass Comes, The Daughter of a Chief, Adventure Comes Smiling, The Wild-Goose Chase, and In the Devil's Frying-Pan. Chapter one rides with Old Applehead Furrman across the mesa from Albuquerque, sniffing a soft spring breeze.

Green grass in sheltered places means calves and roundup time. Applehead owns about a thousand head, yet age has made him content to hire trusted men for the big roundups and skip the hard work. This spring feels different, though. Some stir of ambition or feeling moves in him, and the wide spaces call as they did in his cowpuncher days.
the-phantom-of-the-opera-by-gaston-lerou: Gaston Leroux's The Phantom of the Opera is listed here with a 1909 date. The pages present hold a table of contents only, so the novel itself does not appear. The list names title and copyright pages, a section on the world of Gaston Leroux, and an introduction, then a prologue and chapters. Is It The Ghost?, The New Margarita, Box Five, and Apollo's Lyre appear, and the list ends at chapter fifteen, Christine! Christine! Three other records of the novel carry differing contents lists.
